title: Dying in the Word
hook: he speaks of dying to ego through the Word and living truly

segments.voice: Yesterday, gurmukh and manmukh: two directions of the face, not two kinds of people. Your line was face the good.

Some phrases sound alarming until you see them up close. An argument at the dinner table: someone is sure they're right, and your clever reply is loading. Then, for no reason anyone can see, you let it go. The reply dies unspoken. Something small in you has to lose for the evening to be saved. Guru Amar Das has a bold phrase for a much larger version of that moment: to die in the Word. It sounds like an ending. In his hymns it's the start of living.
screen: `THE CLEVER REPLY, LOADING.` → `SOMETHING SMALL HAS TO LOSE.` → `TO DIE IN THE WORD.`

segments.voice: In Sri Rag he says it like this, paraphrased: whoever dies in the Word stays dead, and does not die a second time. Through the Word the Lord is found, and love for the Name takes hold. So what dies? Not the body. Haumai, the ego, the I, I, mine. The Word, sabad, is the Guru's teaching; dying in it means letting that teaching put something other than me at the center, which ego never allows. Then the strange promise: you don't die a second time. Some readers take it this way: once ego's grip is broken in the Word, the fear of death and the round of coming and going lose their hold. Ten days ago, Guru Angad's salok gave this a picture: dying while alive. Sikhs call it jivat marna. It doesn't mean giving up on life, ever. It means living fully, with the self out of the driver's seat. If dark thoughts about your own life ever come, please call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number. Ego rarely dies in one heroic moment. It dies in dinner-table moments: the reply you don't fire, the credit you don't grab, the grudge you put down. Each is a small rehearsal of the big thing. And the verse is clear about where this leads. Not into gloom. What follows the dying is finding the Lord, and a love for the Name that takes hold.
screen: `DIES IN THE WORD, DIES NO MORE.` · `WHAT DIES: THE EGO'S GRIP.` · `JIVAT MARNA: DYING WHILE ALIVE.` · `SMALL DEATHS AT THE DINNER TABLE.` · then, large: `DIE TO EGO.`

segments.voice: Find one small want that's mostly about being seen, being right or being first, like the last word in a text thread or someone noticing what you did. Look at it gently, then on a long breath out set it down, as many times as it takes. If you pray, let Waheguru fill the space it leaves.
Dying in the Word. Letting ego's grip break through the Guru's teaching, so that, as Guru Amar Das says, you need not die a second time, and can begin to live truly. Today's word.
Your line: die to ego. What lives in its place is the whole point. See you in the morning.

howItsDone: Sikhs meet the idea of dying in the Word in Guru Amar Das's hymns, sung in kirtan and explained in katha; it is lived through daily remembrance of the Name and seva done without seeking credit.

chat.says: 'Die in the Word' sounds scary. Is it about giving up on life?
options: No. It's ego's grip that dies, so you can live fully with the self out of the driver's seat.
Yes. It means leaving the world behind and quietly waiting for the body to die.
No. It means memorizing every word of the hymns so well you never forget one.
chat.meaning: What dies in the Word is ego's grip, not the body. Jivat marna, dying while alive, means living fully, with the Name at the center.
